audience: Children in Grades 4–5 (ages 9–11) who are complete beginners
series_title: Kids Coding with Nova and Pixel

creative_direction.narration: Warm, curious, inclusive, and clear at about 140–145 words per minute; friendly without sounding babyish
creative_direction.visual_language: Bright modern 2D motion graphics, real Scratch or Thonny captures, deterministic code overlays, and a recurring mission map
creative_direction.accessibility: Closed captions (an MP4 caption track plus .srt and .vtt files), Okabe–Ito palette, high contrast, large readable type, no color-only clues, gentle motion, and no rapid flashing
creative_direction.story_world: Nova is an inventive ten-year-old coder. Pixel is a palm-sized helper robot who takes instructions very literally. Nova writes the code and Pixel runs it exactly as written, so when something goes wrong the two investigate together. Each week, the pair opens a new door in the Kids Coding workshop by learning one idea, testing it, and repairing one friendly bug. Learners are invited to predict before the answer appears.

plan_notes: The scripts were written from the Level 3 (Advanced: Python projects, git, objects, algorithms, data and AI) syllabus, teacher guide, all 12 lesson plans, workbook and homework chapters, every exercise brief, starter and hint, and the final project materials, then checked line by line by a separate reviewer against the same sources and the answer keys.

Every code example shown or read aloud was run, and its output and error messages match what Python prints. Examples were chosen so that no video gives away the answer to an exercise, homework, exit ticket, checkpoint question or the project reference; the review replaced several examples that were too close.
Each script names the misconception it prevents, uses the level's own debugging routine and citizenship wording, and points learners to the lesson's first hands-on activity.

videos.title: Save Points with Git
videos.lesson_question: How can git give our code save points that we can go back to?
objectives: Explain that a commit is a save point with a message and a commit id.
Make a commit in Terminal with git add and git commit -m, after setting a nickname with git config.
Describe what git log, git diff and git restore do: look back, spot a change and undo a mistake.
Explain why passwords, real names and other secrets never go into a commit history.
videos.misconception: git add alone makes a save point, or deleting a committed file later also removes it from the history.
videos.safety_and_citizenship: History is public-ish: never commit secrets. Commit with a nickname and an @example.com email; never put passwords, real names, addresses, school names or photos of people in a repository. If a secret ever gets committed, tell a grown-up and change that password: deleting the file is not enough.
videos.lesson_handoff: Open Exercise 1.1 The Git Quest and follow its 7 levels in Terminal: make Documents/git-quest, set a nickname with git config and check it, git init, commit hero_badge.py, change the badge and look at git diff, break the file on purpose and rescue it with git restore, then make a commit of your own. Done looks like git log --oneline showing 3 or more commits with helpful messages.

scenes.purpose: Mission hook
scenes.narration: Welcome to Level 3! Nova is building a rocket game, and it finally works. ‘Let's add a giant laser!’ says Nova. Pixel runs it, exactly as written… and the whole game crashes. Uh-oh. Nova wants the working game back, but it's gone. In a video game, you'd just load a save point. Can code have save points too?
scenes.visual: Workshop. A code panel shows a small rocket game running. Nova types one new line and Pixel presses Run; the panel shakes gently and a red error appears. Nova searches for an undo button. A video-game save icon floats up with a question mark, then freeze on a thinking bubble.
on_screen_text: Pause: When would you want a save?
scenes.production_notes: Three-second prediction pause. Use a soft comic boing for the crash, not a failure buzzer.

scenes.purpose: Explain git, commits and the two-move save
scenes.narration: Good news: a program called git can help. Git takes snapshots of a folder. Each snapshot is a save point called a commit. Every commit has a message that says what changed, and a short code name: a commit id. Making a commit takes two moves, like taking a class photo. First, git add calls files into the photo. Then git commit presses the camera button and adds a caption. git log is the photo album. git diff is spot the difference between now and the last photo. And git restore puts a file back the way it was in the last photo. Pause and point: which command is the camera button?
scenes.visual: A time arrow with commit dots: a1b ‘Start game’, c3d ‘Add hero’, e5f ‘Add jump’. Then a class-photo scene: file cards step into a frame (git add), a camera flash (git commit), and the photo drops into an album (git log). Finish on three labeled boxes, Your folder → Ready to save → History, with a dashed arrow back labeled git restore.
on_screen_text: log = album • diff = spot the difference
scenes.production_notes: Hold the final diagram for four seconds during the pause. Give each box a label and an icon, not color alone.

scenes.purpose: Worked example: a nickname and a first commit
scenes.narration: Let's make Nova's first save point in Terminal. Terminal is a chat window with the computer: you type a command, press Return, and it answers. Nova makes a git-quest folder in Documents and goes inside with cd. Important: git writes your name into every save point, forever. So Nova types git config, dash dash global, user dot name, and a nickname: StarOwl. ‘Never my real name,’ says Nova. The email is pretend too: it ends in example dot com. Nova checks with git config user dot name: StarOwl. Then git init starts the save system. git add rocket dot py calls the file into the photo, and git commit dash m ‘Add rocket drawing’ snaps it. Now git log dash dash oneline shows one line: a commit id and the message. Your id will be different!
scenes.visual: A Terminal panel. Commands type in one at a time: cd ~/Documents, mkdir git-quest, cd git-quest, the two git config lines, git config user.name (answer: StarOwl), git init, git add rocket.py, git commit -m "Add rocket drawing", git log --oneline. The answer line 3b8d2f1 (HEAD -> master) Add rocket drawing appears, and a first commit dot pops onto the timeline. Nova gives Pixel a thumbs-up.
scenes.production_notes: Show the email line exactly as git config --global user.email "starowl@example.com". The commit id is illustrative; add a small caption that master may say main. Do not use hero_badge.py or the Git Quest's own commit messages.

scenes.purpose: Friendly bug hunt: the wrong file and an unhelpful message
scenes.narration: Bug hunt! Nova adds a smoke trail to the rocket and wants to save. Nova types git add rocket dot py, then git add diary dot txt, and is about to commit with the message ‘things’. Wait! First, let's check git status. Changes to be committed: diary dot txt and rocket dot py. Nova's diary has a real name and an address in it. That's the wrong file! And does ‘things’ say what changed? Let's be detectives: read the clue, find the line, guess, and test one change. Fix one: git restore dash dash staged diary dot txt takes the diary out of the photo before it's taken. Check git status again: only rocket dot py is ready to save. Fix two: a message that says what changed, like ‘Add rocket smoke trail’. Nice catch!
scenes.visual: Terminal panel. The two git add lines type in; Nova's hand hovers before a commit, then git status runs instead. Its output appears under ‘Changes to be committed:’ with ‘new file: diary.txt’ then ‘modified: rocket.py’ (git lists them A to Z); a magnifying glass highlights diary.txt and a sticky note shows a blurred name and address. The diary card steps out of the photo frame. The second git status shows only ‘modified: rocket.py’ under ‘Changes to be committed:’, with diary.txt moved down to ‘Untracked files:’. A message card crosses out ‘things’ and writes ‘Add rocket smoke trail’. A check mark appears only after the second git status.
on_screen_text: Run git status before every commit
Say WHAT changed in the message
scenes.production_notes: Leave four seconds for prediction. Do not show the lesson's messy-history board (asdf, stuff, passwords.txt) or the homework's message makeover examples. The blurred diary text must not show any readable name or address.

scenes.purpose: Recap, never commit secrets, and handoff
scenes.narration: Save point unlocked! Let's remember. A commit is a save point with a message and an id. First git add, then git commit. git log is the album, git diff spots the difference, and git restore reloads the last save. And remember: history is public-ish. Git remembers everything, even files you delete later. So commit with a nickname and an example dot com email. Never commit passwords, real names, addresses, school names or photos of people. If a secret ever gets committed, tell a grown-up. Now open The Git Quest. Follow its seven levels, from your first commit to a rescue with git restore. Can you get three commits with helpful messages?
scenes.visual: Mission map: the first door opens. Recap icons for add, commit, log, diff and restore. A safe profile card reads ‘StarOwl, starowl@example.com’, beside crossed-out icons for a password, a house, a school and a photo. End card points to The Git Quest folder.
scenes.production_notes: End card includes ‘Narration uses an AI-generated voice’ and a five-second clean hold for teachers to pause.

videos.title: Blueprints and Objects
videos.lesson_question: How can one class build many objects that each keep their own data?
objectives: Explain that a class is a blueprint and an object is one thing built from it.
Read a class with __init__, attributes and a method, and make two objects from it.
Explain what self means and fix a method that forgets it.
videos.misconception: Changing one object changes every object made from the same class, or the class itself is the object.
videos.safety_and_citizenship: Designing virtual pets kindly: our pets never get sick, run away or make you feel guilty, and never need money or daily streaks. Good games are fun because you want to play, not because they make you feel guilty. Ask: is this fair and kind to the player? Programmers choose how their games treat people.
videos.lesson_handoff: Open Exercise 2.1 Pet Class: __init__ and feed are done. Finish play, mood and describe, then press Run, type p a few times and then f, and watch Pip change while Bo stays the same. Check with check_my_work.py.

scenes.purpose: Mission hook
scenes.narration: Nova wants a garden game with lots and lots of plants. ‘I'll write the code for one plant,’ says Nova, ‘then copy it… and copy it… and copy it.’ Nova starts copying. Fifty copies later, Nova wants plants to grow faster. Uh-oh. That's fifty changes! Can we write the plan once and build as many plants as we like?
scenes.visual: Code panel fills with copy after copy of the same plant code while Nova's typing hands blur and Pixel watches. A counter ticks to 50. Nova holds up a pencil to change one line and gasps at the scrolling wall of copies. Freeze on a thinking bubble.
on_screen_text: Pause: How could we avoid 50 copies?
scenes.production_notes: Three-second prediction pause. Keep the copy wall readable as a pattern, not tiny text.

scenes.purpose: Explain class, object, attribute, method and __init__
scenes.narration: We can! Think of a cookie cutter. One cutter makes lots of cookies, and each cookie can have its own sprinkles and flavor. In Python, the cutter is a class: a blueprint. Each cookie is an object: one thing built from the blueprint. The facts an object remembers are called attributes, like a plant's height. The actions it can do are methods: functions that live inside the class. The setup method has a funny name: dunder init. That's two underscores, init, two underscores. It runs once, every time a new object is made. Pause and point: is the cookie cutter the class or the object?
scenes.visual: A star-shaped cookie cutter labeled ‘class’ stamps three cookies labeled ‘object’, each decorated differently. Each cookie flips to show fact cards (attributes). A blueprint card for Plant appears with an attributes section and a methods section, and the __init__ line glows with two underscores on each side.
on_screen_text: object = one thing built from it
attribute = a fact • method = an action
scenes.production_notes: Show underscores clearly in a monospaced font. Hold four seconds on the question.

scenes.purpose: Worked example: a Plant class and two objects
scenes.narration: Let's build a Plant class. Class Plant, colon. Inside, def dunder init, with self and name. It saves self dot name and sets self dot height to one. Then a method: def water, with self. It says self dot height equals self dot height plus three. So what's self? Self means ‘my.’ Self dot height means ‘my height.’ And Python fills in self for you. Now Nova makes two plants: sunny equals Plant ‘Sunny’, and fern equals Plant ‘Fern’. Pixel runs sunny dot water. Predict! How tall is Sunny now? Four. And Fern? Still one! Nothing happened to Fern. Watering Sunny only changed Sunny. Same blueprint, different objects, and each one keeps its own numbers.
scenes.visual: Code panel: class Plant: / def __init__(self, name): / self.name = name / self.height = 1 / def water(self): / self.height = self.height + 3 / sunny = Plant("Sunny") / fern = Plant("Fern") / sunny.water(). A blueprint card produces two object cards, Sunny and Fern, both height 1. When sunny.water() runs, only Sunny's card ticks to 4 and its sprout grows; Fern's card stays at 1.
scenes.production_notes: Pause three seconds after ‘Predict!’. Do not use the Pet class, Pip and Bo, or the exit-ticket question.

scenes.purpose: Friendly bug hunt: forgot self
scenes.narration: Bug hunt! Nova writes a new version of water, but forgets something. def water, with empty parentheses. Inside: height equals height plus three. Pixel runs sunny dot water, and gets a red error. Let's read it from the bottom up. TypeError: Plant dot water takes zero positional arguments but one was given. Hmm. Python tried to hand the plant to the method, but there was no self to catch it! Guess, and test one change: put self in the parentheses. Run again. A new error: UnboundLocalError. Ask: whose height? Not the plant's! Change one more thing: write self dot height on both sides. Run it. Sunny grows! Every method needs self first.
scenes.visual: Code panel shows def water(): with an empty pair of parentheses glowing. A Shell panel shows the red error; a pointer starts at the bottom line. Pixel holds out a plant card to a method that has no hands to catch it. After the first fix, a second red error appears; a speech bubble asks ‘Whose height?’ and both height words gain self. in front. The rerun shows Sunny's sprout growing, then a check mark.
on_screen_text: Read → find the line → guess → test
scenes.production_notes: Real wording: ‘TypeError: Plant.water() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given’. Do not show Pet.play or happiness (the lesson's bug-hunt station). Allow four seconds for each prediction.

scenes.purpose: Recap, kind pet design, and handoff
scenes.narration: Blueprint built! A class is a blueprint. Objects are the things you build from it, and each one keeps its own attributes. Methods are actions, and self means ‘my.’ Now, a design question. Some pet apps say, ‘Your pet is sad. You forgot it!’ How does that make players feel? Our pets never get sick, never run away, and never make you feel guilty. They never need money or daily streaks, either. Programmers choose how their games treat people. Now open Pet Class. Finish play, mood and describe. Then press Run and play with Pip. Does Bo change too? Find out!
scenes.visual: Mission map: the second door opens. Recap icons: blueprint, two object cards, an action arrow. A gentle virtual pet waves next to a crossed-out guilt-trip pop-up and a crossed-out coin and calendar streak. End card points to the Pet Class folder.
scenes.production_notes: End card includes ‘Narration uses an AI-generated voice’ and a five-second clean hold for teachers to pause.

videos.title: Families of Objects
videos.lesson_question: How can classes share code in families, and how can objects be built from other objects?
objectives: Explain how a child class inherits from a parent and uses super().__init__ to reuse the parent's setup.
Override a method so different classes react differently to the same call.
Tell inheritance (is a) from composition (has a) by saying the sentence aloud.
Find a missing super().__init__ call and a misspelled override.
videos.misconception: A child class must copy all of its parent's code, or a misspelled method name still replaces the parent's method.
videos.safety_and_citizenship: Representation: who gets to be the hero? Designing a character family is a chance to include many kinds of people: different names, skin tones, ages and abilities. Avoid making one group always the villain or always the helper.
videos.lesson_handoff: Open Exercise 3.1 Enemy Family: read Enemy and Guard first, then finish Zigzagger.move (use super().move()), Sprinter.__init__ (use super().__init__), Sprinter.move and move_all. Run prints 4 turns, and check_my_work.py passes.

scenes.purpose: Mission hook
scenes.narration: Nova's robot workshop is growing. There's a plain Robot that rolls one step at a time. Now Nova wants a PaintBot that rolls and paints, and lots more kinds after that. ‘Do I have to copy the whole Robot class every time?’ asks Nova. Pixel holds up a family tree. What if robots could have families?
scenes.visual: Workshop floor with one plain robot rolling a step. Nova sketches more robot kinds on a whiteboard, looking worried at a tall stack of copied code. Pixel unrolls a family-tree poster. Freeze on the poster.
on_screen_text: Pause: What do all robots share?
scenes.production_notes: Three-second prediction pause.

scenes.purpose: Explain inheritance, overriding, super() and composition
scenes.narration: They can! A child class inherits everything from its parent class: all its attributes and methods. Then it changes only what is different. Think of Grandma's pancake recipe. Your recipe says: make Grandma's pancakes, then add blueberries. You don't copy her whole recipe. You use it and add one thing. Changing a method in the child is called overriding. And super means ‘my parent.’ One more way to build: a Workshop isn't a kind of Robot, but a Workshop has Robots. That's composition. Say the sentence aloud. Is a means inheritance. Has a means composition.
scenes.visual: A family tree of classes: a Robot parent card at the top (name, x, move) with is-a arrows from two child cards, PaintBot (adds color) and a blank card with a question mark. A recipe card ‘Grandma's pancakes’ gets a sticky note ‘+ blueberries’. Then a Workshop box opens to show robot cards inside it, labeled has a.
scenes.production_notes: Use arrows with an open triangle head for is a and a containing box for has a, so the two ideas differ by shape as well as label.

scenes.purpose: Worked example: a PaintBot is a Robot
scenes.narration: Here's the parent: class Robot. Its setup saves a name and an x position, and move adds one to x. Now the child: class PaintBot, with Robot in parentheses. That means a PaintBot is a Robot. PaintBot's setup calls super dot dunder init with name and x. ‘Parent, set up your part!’ says Nova. Then the child adds its extra: a color. PaintBot also overrides move. First, super dot move does the parent's step. Then it adds its own part: a paint message. Nova makes juno equals PaintBot ‘Juno’, with color green. Pixel runs juno dot move. Predict! x becomes one, and it prints: Juno paints a green dot. A plain Robot and a PaintBot both understand move, but each does it its own way. That's polymorphism: many shapes.
scenes.visual: Code panel: class Robot: with __init__(self, name, x=0) saving self.name and self.x, and move adding 1 to self.x; class PaintBot(Robot): with __init__(self, name, x=0, color="blue") calling super().__init__(name, x) then self.color = color, and move calling super().move() then print(self.name, "paints a", self.color, "dot"). Below: juno = PaintBot("Juno", color="green") and juno.move(). Shell shows Juno paints a green dot. A plain robot and Juno roll side by side; only Juno leaves a green dot.
on_screen_text: Shell: Juno paints a green dot
scenes.production_notes: Highlight each super line as it is read. Do not show Sprinter, Zigzagger, Hero or Owl code (exercise, workbook and homework).

scenes.purpose: Friendly bug hunt: missing super().__init__ and an override typo
scenes.narration: Bug hunt! Nova makes a quick copy of PaintBot, and it has two family bugs. Bug one: the child's setup forgot the super dunder init line. It only saves the color. Pixel runs juno dot move and gets AttributeError: ‘PaintBot’ object has no attribute ‘x’. Read it from the bottom up. No x? The parent's setup never ran! Test one change: put the super line back. Run again. No crash! But wait… Juno rolls and never paints. No error at all. That's a silent bug. Look closely at the method's name: m, o, o, v, e. Moove! That doesn't match, so Python used the parent's move. Fix the spelling and test. Override names must match exactly.
scenes.visual: Code panel of the buggy copy: __init__ with only self.color = color, and def moove(self):. A red AttributeError appears in the Shell; a pointer reads it from the bottom. The family tree shows the Robot setup box grayed out. After the fix, Juno rolls without painting; a magnifier spells m-o-o-v-e letter by letter beside the parent's m-o-v-e. After the spelling fix, Juno paints a green dot and a check mark appears.
scenes.production_notes: Real wording: ‘AttributeError: 'PaintBot' object has no attribute 'x'’ (super().move() reads self.x first). Do not use the lesson's Sprinter/mvoe station, Hexagon, or Diamond/drow (Week 6 Bug Hunt 4). Allow four seconds for each prediction.

scenes.purpose: Recap, representation, and handoff
scenes.narration: Family reunion! A child class inherits from its parent and changes only what is different. super runs the parent's part. Overriding replaces a method, so the same call can do different things. That's polymorphism. And has a means composition. Now, a question for game makers: who gets to be the hero? When you design a character family, include many kinds of people: different names, skin tones, ages and abilities. Don't make one group always the villain or always the helper. Now open Enemy Family. Finish the Zigzagger, the Sprinter and move all. Then press Run. Does every enemy move its own way?
scenes.visual: Mission map: the third door opens. Recap icons: family tree, a super arrow pointing up, a workshop box. A line-up of diverse, friendly game heroes of different ages, skin tones and abilities. End card points to the Enemy Family folder.
scenes.production_notes: End card includes ‘Narration uses an AI-generated voice’ and a five-second clean hold for teachers to pause.

videos.title: Searching: How Fast Is Fast?
videos.lesson_question: How can a smart search do less work than checking one by one?
objectives: Explain linear search and binary search, and why binary search needs a sorted list.
Trace a binary search with low, high and mid.
Count worst-case binary search steps by halving again and again.
Find and fix an off-by-one bug in a binary search.
videos.misconception: Binary search works on any list, or a list ten times bigger needs ten times more binary search steps.
videos.safety_and_citizenship: Search engines and filter bubbles: a search engine ranks results, putting first what it thinks you want based on what you clicked before, so two people can search the same words and see different answers. To get out of a bubble, use different search words, look at several sources, ask a grown-up or a librarian, and notice when something is an ad.
videos.lesson_handoff: Open Exercise 4.1 Search Race: linear_search is done. Write binary_search so it returns (index, steps), predict the binary steps for 10000 items with a halving ladder, then Run to see the race table and check with check_my_work.py.

scenes.purpose: Mission hook
scenes.narration: Pixel has a row of number cards, face down, sorted from smallest to largest. ‘Find the 40!’ says Nova. Pixel flips the first card. Then the next. Then the next. Flip, flip, flip… seven flips! ‘There has to be a faster way,’ says Nova. Can you find a number with fewer flips?
scenes.visual: Seven face-down cards in a row on the workbench. Pixel flips them one at a time from the left while a flip counter ticks up to 7; the last card shows 40. Nova taps a stopwatch. Freeze on a thinking bubble.
on_screen_text: MISSION: Find it in fewer flips
Pause: Which card would you flip first?
scenes.production_notes: Three-second prediction pause. Card numbers stay hidden until flipped.

scenes.purpose: Explain linear search, binary search and the worst case
scenes.narration: Pixel just did a linear search: check the items one by one, from the start. It works on any list, but a long list means a long search. Binary search is smarter. Look at the middle card. If it's too small, the answer must be on the right, so throw away the whole left half. Then check the middle of what's left. Every step cuts the list in half. But there's one rule: the list must be sorted. To compare algorithms, we count the steps in the worst case: the unluckiest search. It's like finding a word in a dictionary. You open it in the middle, not on page one!
scenes.visual: Left side: a pointer walks card by card (linear). Right side: a pointer jumps to the middle card, the left half fades to gray, then it jumps to the middle of what is left. A shuffled row appears with a ‘not sorted’ stop sign. A dictionary opens in the middle.
on_screen_text: Binary search needs a sorted list
scenes.production_notes: Gray thrown-away cards also get a dashed outline so they do not rely on color alone.

scenes.purpose: Worked example: trace a binary search
scenes.narration: Let's trace it. Seven cards: 4, 9, 12, 18, 25, 31, 40. Their places are zero to six. We're looking for 40. Low is zero and high is six. The middle place, mid, is three: add low and high, halve it, and round down. Card three is 18. Too small! So low jumps to four. Now mid is five: card 31. Still too small, so low jumps to six. Now low and high are both six, and there's still one card left to check. Mid is six: 40. Found it! Three steps instead of seven. How many steps for fifty cards? Halve again and again: 50, 25, 12, 6, 3, 1. That's six numbers, so six steps at most.
scenes.visual: The seven cards face up with places 0 to 6 underneath. Pointer cards labeled low, high and mid slide along. A trace table fills one row per step (low, high, mid, card, so…). Thrown-away cards gray out with a dashed outline. Then a halving ladder of number blocks shrinks: 50, 25, 12, 6, 3, 1, counted with ticks.
scenes.production_notes: Do not use the workbook list [3, 8, 15, 21, 29, 37, 44, 52], the homework list [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13], the secret number 73, or the 1000, 10000 and 1,000,000 halvings (exit ticket, exercise and homework predictions). Do not show the binary_search code.

scenes.purpose: Friendly bug hunt: an off-by-one that loops forever
scenes.narration: Bug hunt! Nova writes a binary search, but one line is off by one. When the middle card is too small, it says: low equals mid. Pixel searches for 18 in four cards: 4, 9, 12, 18. Mid is one: 9. Too small, so low becomes one. Mid is two: 12. Too small, so low becomes two. Mid is two again: 12. And again. And again! Pixel is stuck in a loop forever. In Thonny, press the red Stop button. Now let's guess. We already checked the middle card, and it was too small, so we should throw it away too. Test one change: low equals mid plus one. Run it. Found 18! An off-by-one bug is a number that's one too big or one too small.
scenes.visual: Code panel highlights the single line low = mid. Four cards with places 0 to 3; the mid pointer lands on 12 again and again while Pixel spins in a little circle and a loop counter climbs. A finger presses Thonny's red Stop button. The line changes to low = mid + 1; the rerun lands on 18 with a check mark.
on_screen_text: Throw away mid too: low = mid + 1
scenes.production_notes: Use this ‘low = mid’ bug only. Do not show while low < high or high = len(items): they are the lesson's bug-hunt station and Week 6 Bug Hunt 3. Allow four seconds for prediction before the fix.

scenes.purpose: Recap, filter bubbles, and handoff
scenes.narration: Search solved! Linear search checks one by one. Binary search checks the middle and throws away half, but only on a sorted list. Bigger lists need only a few more binary steps. Search engines are super fast, but they also rank the results, putting first what they think you want, based on what you clicked before. So two people can search the same words and see different answers. That's a filter bubble. To get out, try different search words, look at several sources, and ask a grown-up or a librarian. Now open Search Race. Write binary search, and predict its steps for ten thousand items before you run it!
scenes.visual: Mission map: the fourth door opens. Recap icons: a walking pointer and a halving pointer. Two kids type the same search words and get different result cards inside two soap bubbles; the bubbles pop as new sources and a librarian icon appear. End card points to the Search Race folder.
on_screen_text: Sorted list → check the middle → halve
scenes.production_notes: End card includes ‘Narration uses an AI-generated voice’ and a five-second clean hold for teachers to pause. Do not state the step count the program reports for 10000 items.

videos.title: Sorting, Stacks and Queues
videos.lesson_question: How do sorts put data in order, and when do we use a stack or a queue?
objectives: Trace bubble sort and selection sort on four cards and count their swaps.
Explain a stack as last in, first out and a queue as first in, first out.
Swap two values without losing one, and spot a sort that loses items.
Suggest ways to make a leaderboard fair and kind.
videos.misconception: Writing a = b and then b = a swaps two values, or two sorts do the same amount of work because they give the same answer.
videos.safety_and_citizenship: Leaderboards: fair and kind. Show nicknames only, never real names; give ties the same place; show personal bests and most improved, not only the winners; let players choose not to appear. A leaderboard should make people want to play again, not feel bad.
videos.lesson_handoff: Open Exercise 5.1 Sort Race: selection_sort is done. Finish the swap inside bubble_sort and count each swap, then Run it to sort the cards both ways, write down the swaps each sort reports, and check with check_my_work.py.

scenes.purpose: Mission hook
scenes.narration: Nova's game needs three things: a high-score board in order, an undo button, and a fair way to take turns. Pixel stares at a messy pile of score cards and blinks. ‘Where do I even start?’ beeps Pixel. Today we'll sort cards, stack plates and line up for lunch. Ready? Let's go!

on_screen_text: MISSION: Sort it, undo it, take turns
scenes.production_notes: Keep the hook light and quick; no prediction pause needed.

scenes.purpose: Explain two sorts, a stack and a queue
scenes.narration: Sorting means putting things in order, like smallest to largest. Here are two ways. Selection sort finds the smallest card and swaps it to the front. Then it finds the smallest of the rest, and so on. Bubble sort compares two neighbors. If the left one is bigger, they swap. Big cards bubble to the end, like bubbles rising in a drink. Both sorts give the same answer, but they do different amounts of work. Two more helpers. A stack is a pile of plates: last in, first out, just like undo. A queue is a lunch line: first in, first out, so everyone gets a fair turn.
scenes.visual: Number cards demonstrate each rule: a spotlight finds the smallest card and it swaps to the front; then two neighbor cards compare and swap as a bubble floats up. A plate is pushed onto a stack and the top one popped off, with an undo arrow. A short lunch line: someone joins at the back and the front person leaves.
scenes.production_notes: Label push, pop, front and back with words and arrows, not color alone.

scenes.purpose: Worked example: race two sorts on four cards
scenes.narration: Let's race on four cards: 6, 9, 2, 4. Bubble sort first. Compare 6 and 9: keep. 9 and 2: swap. 9 and 4: swap. After pass one, 9 has bubbled to the end. Pass two: 6 and 2, swap. 6 and 4, swap. Now 6 is in place too. Pass three: 2 and 4, keep. Sorted: 2, 4, 6, 9. That's four swaps. Now selection sort, on the same cards. The smallest is 2, so it swaps with 6. One swap. The next smallest is 4, so it swaps with 9. Then 6 is already in place. That's two swaps in all. Same answer, different amount of work! Pause and point: which sort swapped less?
scenes.visual: Bars with numbers on them for 6, 9, 2, 4. Bubble sort: two neighbor bars glow, swap or stay, and a swap counter ticks; bars in their final place get a thick border. Then the same four bars reset for selection sort: a spotlight finds the smallest, swaps it to the front, and a second counter ticks. Both counters sit side by side at the end.
scenes.production_notes: Do not use the lesson's 5, 2, 4, 1, the workbook's 4, 1, 3, 2, the mid-level checkpoint's 7, 3, 9, 1, or the exercise cards [7, 3, 9, 1, 5, 3, 8, 2] and their swap counts. Do not show the bubble_sort code.

scenes.purpose: Friendly bug hunt: the swap that loses an item
scenes.narration: Bug hunt! Nova wants two cards to trade places. Left is 9, and right is 4. Nova writes: left equals right. Then: right equals left. Pixel runs it and prints both: 4 and 4! Where did the 9 go? Let's act it out. The first line puts a 4 where the 9 was, and the 9 is gone. The second line just copies that 4 back. A sort with this swap loses items! Guess, and test one change: Python can swap both at once. left comma right equals right comma left. Run it: 4 and 9. Nothing lost! One more clue: if a high-score board shows the lowest score on top, check the order. For biggest first, sorted needs reverse equals True.
scenes.visual: Two card slots labeled left and right holding 9 and 4. Line one: a 4 card drops onto the 9 slot and the 9 card puffs away; line two copies 4 into the right slot. The Shell prints 4 4. Pixel acts it out with two real cards. The fix line slides in and both cards cross paths at the same time; the Shell prints 4 9. Then a small score board flips from lowest-first to biggest-first when reverse=True is added.
scenes.production_notes: Code: left = 9 / right = 4 / left = right / right = left / print(left, right) prints 4 4; with left, right = right, left it prints 4 9. Do not show the lesson's [5, 2] station, the result[i] swap, or the Week 6 Lost Scores bugs. Allow four seconds for prediction.

scenes.purpose: Recap, fair leaderboards, and handoff
scenes.narration: Cards sorted! Selection sort swaps the smallest to the front. Bubble sort swaps neighbors. A stack is last in, first out, and a queue is first in, first out. Now let's talk about leaderboards. How would you feel if you were always at the bottom of a board everyone can see? A fair, kind board shows nicknames only, never real names. Ties share the same place. It celebrates personal bests and most improved, not only the winners. And players can choose not to appear. Now open Sort Race. Finish the swap inside bubble sort, run it, and write down how many swaps each sort makes.

videos.title: Slow-Motion Debugging
videos.lesson_question: How can the Thonny debugger help us watch our code think, one line at a time?
objectives: Use Debug, Step over, Step into and the Variables view to follow a program one line at a time.
Follow the bug-hunting loop: read, predict, watch, fix one thing, check.
Connect the big ideas from weeks 1 to 5: save points, classes, families, searching and sorting.
Describe a hard bug, what helped, and how to ask for help clearly.
videos.misconception: Pressing Run shows what happens inside the code, or changing several lines at once is the fastest way to fix a bug.
videos.safety_and_citizenship: Growth mindset: bugs are how we learn. Every programmer meets bugs every day; celebrate effort and strategy, not speed. Asking for help with a clear description (what I expected, what happened, what I tried) is a skill, not a weakness, and being kind when a partner's code is broken is part of being a good teammate.
videos.lesson_handoff: Open Bug Hunt 1: Score Keeper (three bugs, all the same kind). Press Run and read the last line of the red error, then use Debug, Step into and Step over with the Variables view; fix one bug, run again, and repeat until Run prints Comet has 10 points and check_my_work.py passes.

scenes.purpose: Mission hook
scenes.narration: Checkpoint week! Nova and Pixel look back at their quest map: save points, blueprints, families, searching and sorting. But today, Nova's code does something strange, and it happens too fast to see. ‘I wish I could slow it down,’ says Nova. What if you could watch your code think, one line at a time?
scenes.visual: The mission map with five opened doors, each with an icon: a commit dot, a blueprint, a family tree, a halving pointer, sorted bars. A sixth door is marked with a magnifying glass. Nova's program flashes past in a blur, and a pause icon appears.
on_screen_text: Pause: Where could a bug hide?
scenes.production_notes: Three-second prediction pause.

scenes.purpose: Explain the Thonny debugger buttons
scenes.narration: You can, with a debugger. A debugger is a slow-motion replay for your code. It's like the replay of a soccer goal: you can pause on every frame and see where every player is. In Thonny, click Debug, the bug icon next to the green Run button. The first line lights up. The highlighted line is the one that runs next. Step over runs that line and stops at the next one. Step into goes inside a function call, so you can watch its lines too. Turn on View, then Variables, to see every variable's value right now. And Stop, the red sign, ends the program.
scenes.visual: A soccer replay freezes on a frame with player labels. Then a clean Thonny toolbar: Run, Debug, Step over, Step into, Resume and Stop, each labeled under its icon as it is named. The highlight moves down a short program one line at a time, and the Variables panel opens with View > Variables.
on_screen_text: Step over: run this line, stop at next
Step into: go inside a function
scenes.production_notes: Use an authentic current Thonny capture with labels as overlays outside it. Mention on screen that the toolbar buttons work on every Mac, even when the F-keys need fn.

scenes.purpose: Worked example: step into a method
scenes.narration: Let's try it on a tiny Robot class. Its setup gives every robot a battery of fifty, and charge adds some power. At the bottom, Nova makes bolt and calls bolt dot charge twenty-five. Nova clicks Debug, and the first line lights up. Step over, step over… In the Variables view, bolt appears. Click it, and the Object inspector shows its attributes: battery is fifty. Now the highlighted line calls charge, one of our own methods. So Nova clicks Step into. A small window opens. That's normal: it shows the method's own variables, like power, which is twenty-five. Step over once more, and battery becomes seventy-five. Back outside, print shows 75. We watched every step!
scenes.visual: Code panel: class Robot: / def __init__(self, name): / self.name = name / self.battery = 50 / def charge(self, power): / self.battery = self.battery + power / bolt = Robot("Bolt") / bolt.charge(25) / print(bolt.battery). A highlight bar walks down the lines. The Variables panel shows bolt; the Object inspector shows battery 50. On Step into, a small method window opens showing power 25; battery ticks to 75. The Shell prints 75. Pixel watches with a tiny replay remote.
scenes.production_notes: Turn on View > Variables and View > Object inspector before recording. Do not use ScoreKeeper, undo_last or PiggyBank code (Bug Hunt 1 and Homework 6), or their numbers 10, 5 and 15 and the parameter name amount (the deposit fix).

scenes.purpose: Friendly bug hunt: the total that keeps resetting
scenes.narration: Bug-hunt workshop! Nova wants to add up coins: 3, 4 and 5 should make 12. But the program prints 5. There's no red error this time, so let's use the bug-hunting loop. One, read: we expected 12, but got 5. Two, predict: ‘I think the total line is wrong,’ says Nova. Three, watch: click Debug and step over. Total becomes 3, then jumps back to zero, then 4. Then zero again! Aha! The line total equals zero is inside the loop, so it runs every time. Four, fix one thing: move that line above the loop. Five, check: run it. 12! If it's still failing, go around the loop again. Nice catch!
scenes.visual: Code panel: for coin in [3, 4, 5]: / total = 0 / total = total + coin / print(total) (print is not indented, so it runs once after the loop). The Shell prints 5 next to an expected card saying 12. A five-step loop diagram (Read, Predict, Watch, Fix ONE thing, Check) lights up one step at a time. In the Variables panel, total flips 0, 3, 0, 4, 0, 5 like a scoreboard. The total = 0 line slides up above the for line; the rerun prints 12 and a check mark appears.
scenes.production_notes: Do not show any Week 6 bug-hunt station or Homework 6 bug (missing self, list copy, while condition, duplicates, high = len, low < high, missing call parentheses, super, drow, deposit, withdraw or statement). Allow four seconds for prediction.

scenes.purpose: Recap, growth mindset, and handoff
scenes.narration: Checkpoint reached! A debugger is a slow-motion replay. Debug starts it, Step over runs one line, Step into goes inside your method, and the Variables view shows every value. When a bug appears: read, predict, watch, fix one thing, and check. Now, a secret: every programmer meets bugs every day. Bugs are how we learn! If you get stuck, ask for help clearly: what I expected, what happened, what I tried. That's a skill, not a weakness. And be kind when a partner's code is broken. Now open Bug Hunt 1, Score Keeper. Run it, read the last line of the error, and debug one fix at a time. Happy hunting!

videos.title: Grids, Recursion and Fractal Art
videos.lesson_question: How can a function solve a big problem by calling itself on a smaller copy of the same problem?
objectives: Explain recursion as solving a smaller copy of the same problem, and point to the base case and the recursive case.
Read one cell of a grid with grid[row][col]: row first, then column, both counted from 0.
Describe how a fractal tree is made of smaller copies of itself and how a paint bucket spreads to neighbors.
Find and fix a missing base case when Python shows a RecursionError.
videos.misconception: A function that calls itself will somehow know when to stop on its own, or grid[row][col] works like turtle's (x, y) with across first.
videos.safety_and_citizenship: Credit for generative art and algorithms: the fractal tree and the Koch snowflake (Helge von Koch, 1904) are famous ideas. When you show generative art, say where the idea came from: ‘Fractal tree, based on a classic recursive algorithm; my colors and angles.’ Your code is yours; the idea has a history; giving credit is what real artists and programmers do. Add a comment line # Based on: ... at the top of your fractal file.
videos.lesson_handoff: Type along with your teacher in Exercise 7.2 Fractal tree: run starter.py (only the trunks appear), read the base case aloud, add the five TODO lines after the trunk (turn left, smaller tree, turn right twice as far, smaller tree, turn back) and count the lines at depth 1, 2 and 3. Then, in pairs, finish Exercise 7.1 Recursion warm-up (sum_to(n), so sum_to(5) is 15, and reverse(word), so reverse("turtle") is "eltrut", each with a base case and a recursive case; check with check_my_work.py) and build the paint bucket in 7.3.

scenes.purpose: Mission hook
scenes.narration: Welcome back to Kids Coding! Today Nova wants two things: a whole forest of trees drawn by code, and a paint bucket that fills a pixel picture with one click. ‘That sounds like thousands of lines,’ beeps Pixel. ‘Not if a function can call itself,’ says Nova. Wait… a function that calls itself? Can it ever stop?
scenes.visual: Workshop door 7. Nova sketches a forest and a pixel picture on a whiteboard; Pixel stacks a towering pile of code pages that wobbles. Nova holds up one small recipe card. Freeze on Pixel's puzzled face and a big question mark.
on_screen_text: MISSION: A forest and a paint bucket
Pause: Can a function call itself?
scenes.production_notes: Three-second prediction pause after the question. Gentle wobble, no crash sound.

scenes.purpose: Explain recursion: base case and recursive case
scenes.narration: Picture a set of Russian dolls. Your job is: open the doll. Inside is a smaller doll, so your job is the same again. You keep going until you reach the tiny solid doll. It can't open, so you stop. That's recursion: a function that calls itself on a smaller problem. Every recursive function has two parts. The recursive case does one small step, then calls itself on something smaller. The base case is the tiny problem you can answer straight away, so you stop. Look at countdown. If n is zero or less, print Liftoff and return. That's the base case. Otherwise, print n, then call countdown with n minus one.
scenes.visual: Nested dolls open one inside the next; the last solid doll glows with a STOP badge labeled 'base case'. Then the countdown code from the Exercise 7.1 starter appears in a Thonny panel: the if-block is boxed in orange and labeled 'base case', and the countdown(n - 1) line is boxed in sky blue and labeled 'recursive case'.
on_screen_text: Recursive case = small step + call again
scenes.production_notes: Show countdown exactly as in the starter (finished code). Never show sum_to or reverse code: they are Exercise 7.1's TODOs.

scenes.purpose: Worked example: stacked calls, a fractal tree and a grid
scenes.narration: Let's watch countdown of three run. It prints three, then calls countdown of two, which waits inside it like a smaller doll. Two, one… then countdown of zero reaches the base case: Liftoff! A fractal is a shape made of smaller copies of itself. A tree is a trunk with two smaller trees on top, until the depth reaches zero. Depth one is one line. Depth two, three lines. Depth three, seven. Now grids. A grid is a list of rows, and each row is a list. grid, row one, column three, means go down to row one, then across to column three, both counted from zero. Like a movie ticket: row first, then seat. That cell is H. A paint bucket paints one square, then asks each neighbor, up, down, left and right, to do the same. Where should the paint stop? You'll work that out in Exercise 7.3!
scenes.visual: Russian-doll style nested call boxes slide out: countdown(3) → countdown(2) → countdown(1) → countdown(0), each printing its line in a Shell strip, then the boxes close back up. Next, a fractal tree grows branch by branch beside a counter: depth 1 = 1 line, depth 2 = 3 lines, depth 3 = 7 lines. Last, a 3-by-4 grid of letters A–L with row numbers down the side and column numbers across the top; a finger walks down to row 1, then across to column 3, and H lights up. A paint drop lands on one cell and arrows point up, down, left and right, then a big question mark appears.
scenes.production_notes: Use this made-up letter grid, not the workbook's island grid, and stop the line counts at depth 3 (depth 3 = 7 is printed in the workbook picture and the 7.2 README; the workbook table's depth 4 and 5 blanks and the exit ticket's depth 4 are answers). Do not show the fractal tree's five TODO lines or the flood fill's base case and calls.

scenes.purpose: Friendly bug hunt: missing base case (RecursionError)
scenes.narration: Bug hunt! Nova writes a function called open_doll. It prints ‘Opening doll’ and the size, then calls open_doll with the size minus one. Pixel runs open_doll of three. Three, two, one, zero, minus one, minus two… the numbers keep falling below zero, and then a red error appears. Let's use our bug-hunting steps. One, read the last line of the error: RecursionError, maximum recursion depth exceeded. Two, predict. ‘I think it never stops,’ says Nova. RecursionError? Look for the base case first! Three, watch: in the debugger, Step into, and the calls pile up like plates. Four, fix one thing. Nova adds a base case: if size is zero, print ‘Solid doll!’ and return. Five, check: run it again. Opening doll three, two, one, Solid doll!
scenes.visual: Code panel with the three-line open_doll function and the call open_doll(3). The Shell scrolls: Opening doll 3, 2, 1, 0, -1, -2… as nesting-doll icons shrink to dots, then the red last line. Five step cards light up in turn: Read, Predict, Watch, Fix ONE thing, Check. Thonny's debugger shows boxes stacking. The fix inserts an if-block at the top of the function; the rerun prints four lines and Pixel gives a thumbs-up.
on_screen_text: RecursionError? Find the base case first
Read • Predict • Watch • Fix one • Check
scenes.production_notes: Four-second prediction pause before the fix appears. Use open_doll only; never show sum_to without a base case (the lesson's bug hunt) or its fix, which is Exercise 7.1's answer. Exact fixed code: if size == 0: print("Solid doll!") then return, above the print line.

scenes.purpose: Recap, credit for generative art, and handoff
scenes.narration: Door seven unlocked! Recursion means a function calls itself on a smaller problem. The base case says stop, and the recursive case does one small step and calls itself again. A grid is a list of rows: row first, then column. The fractal tree is a famous idea, and the Koch snowflake was invented by Helge von Koch in 1904. When you show generative art, say where the idea came from, like ‘Fractal tree, based on a classic recursive algorithm; my colors and angles.’ Add a comment that starts with Based on at the top of your file. Now open Exercise 7.2, the Fractal tree, and type along with your teacher. Then finish sum_to and reverse in Exercise 7.1. Where's your base case? Happy coding!

videos.title: Data Detectives: Clean, Count, Chart
videos.lesson_question: How do we turn a messy file of survey answers into a true story we can count and chart?
objectives: Read a CSV file with csv.DictReader and clean it: strip spaces, skip empty rows, turn text into numbers.
Count answers with a dictionary tally and work out an average that skips missing answers.
Describe a bar chart where every bar has its name and its number written on it, not color alone.
Explain why surveys need consent and how to anonymize answers before sharing.
videos.misconception: Numbers read from a CSV file are already numbers, or a blank answer should count as 0 in an average.
videos.safety_and_citizenship: Consent and anonymizing survey data: our survey asked first, let people pass, and had no names. That is consent and anonymity. Even without names, some answers together can point to one person (the only 13-year-old in the chess club). Before sharing data: keep only the columns you need, replace names with IDs like R1, R2, and never collect addresses, schools, birthdays or photos.
videos.lesson_handoff: Type along with your teacher in Exercise 8.1 Survey cleaner: open starter.py and favorite_games.csv, circle the mess (extra spaces, MiXeD capitals, empty rows, a missing number), then finish to_number() and is_empty() and add .title() to the game names, until the Shell says Clean answers: 17 instead of 19. Then, in pairs, count and average in 8.2 and draw the labeled bar chart in 8.3.

scenes.purpose: Mission hook
scenes.narration: Nova ran a survey: ‘What's your favorite pet?’ Everyone could choose to answer or pass, and nobody wrote their name. Now the answers are in a file, and Pixel proudly reports: ‘Cat and CAT are two different pets!’ Hmm. That doesn't sound right. How can a data detective find the true story in messy answers?
scenes.visual: Nova drops folded sticky notes into a box marked ‘No names. You can pass.’ The notes fly into a text file. Pixel holds up two signs, ‘Cat’ and ‘CAT’, with a proud beep. Nova raises an eyebrow; a detective magnifying glass appears.
on_screen_text: Pause: Are Cat and CAT the same?
scenes.production_notes: Keep the survey anonymous on screen: no faces or names on any note.

scenes.purpose: Explain the data pipeline and CSV files
scenes.narration: Data detectives always work in the same order: read, clean, count, calculate, chart. First, read. A CSV file, short for comma-separated values, is a table saved as plain text. One line is one row, and commas split the columns. The first line is the header: the column names. Python's csv dot DictReader turns each row into a dictionary, so row, pet, in square brackets, gives that row's answer. Next, clean. Data is like vegetables from the garden: you wash off the mud before you cook. Strip extra spaces, fix MiXeD capitals, and throw away empty rows. Only then do we count, average and chart.
scenes.visual: A five-step pipeline slides in: 1 Read, 2 Clean, 3 Count, 4 Calculate, 5 Chart, each with an icon and a label. A plain-text file morphs into a table: header row highlighted, commas turning into column lines. One row pops out as a dictionary bubble. Muddy carrots get washed as messy values tidy up.
on_screen_text: CSV = a table saved as plain text
scenes.production_notes: Name csv.DictReader correctly. Keep the pet file visibly different from favorite_games.csv.

scenes.purpose: Worked example: clean, tally, fair-share average, chart
scenes.narration: Here's Nova's little file. Row two says space, cat, space. Row three is empty. Row four, Dog, has no minutes. After cleaning with strip and title, every spelling becomes Cat with a capital C, and the empty row is skipped. Now count with a dictionary, like a tally chart. A new pet starts at zero, then we add one. At the end: Cat, three. Dog, one. Next, the average minutes. The average is a fair share: put everything in one pile, then share it equally. Twenty plus ten plus thirty is sixty. Three people answered, so sixty divided by three is twenty. And the blank? A blank means ‘we don't know,’ not zero, so we skip it. Last, the chart. Cat gets the tallest bar. Dog has one vote and Cat has three, so Dog's bar is one third as tall. Write the name under every bar and the number on top.
scenes.visual: A CSV table with columns response, pet, minutes_playing: 1, Cat, 20 / 2, ' cat ', 10 / 3, (empty) / 4, Dog, (blank) / 5, CAT, 30. The empty row is highlighted and slides away; the three cat spellings turn into 'Cat'. A tally chart fills: Cat ||| and Dog |. Counters for 20, 10 and 30 pile into 60 and split into three equal stacks of 20, while the blank cell shows a '?' tag that steps aside. A turtle bar chart draws two bars, Cat 3 and Dog 1, each with its name below and number on top.
on_screen_text: Every bar: name below, number on top
scenes.production_notes: Do not show the counts.get line, the average function or bar_height code: they are Exercise 8.2 and 8.3 TODOs. Do not use the exercise's numbers (Block Craft, 3.1 hours, the 2, 4, 6 helper or the exit ticket's 4, 2, 6).

scenes.purpose: Friendly bug hunt: numbers read as strings and empty answers
scenes.narration: Bug hunt! Nova's minutes came straight from a file: quote ten, quote nine, quote seven. Pixel finds the biggest with max, and max says quote nine. Nine is bigger than ten? Then sum crashes with a red error. Let's use our steps. Read the last line: TypeError, unsupported operand types for plus, int and str. Predict. ‘I think these numbers are really words,’ says Nova. Watch: each number has quote marks around it. Every CSV value arrives as text, and text is compared letter by letter. Fix one thing: turn text into numbers while cleaning. int of quote ten gives the number ten. But careful! int of an empty answer crashes with a ValueError, so a blank becomes None, and we skip it. Check: run again. The biggest is ten, and the total is twenty-six.
scenes.visual: Thonny Shell: minutes = ["10", "9", "7"]. max(minutes) prints '9' with a puzzled Pixel; sum(minutes) prints the red TypeError. The quote marks around each value pulse. The five step cards light up: Read, Predict, Watch, Fix ONE thing, Check. A converter machine turns "10" into 10. An empty answer "" bounces off with a ValueError tag and becomes a None card that steps aside. The rerun shows 10 and 26 with a green check.
scenes.production_notes: Four-second prediction pause before the fix. Use these minutes, not the lesson's hours example. Never show the to_number or is_empty code from Exercise 8.1.

scenes.purpose: Recap, consent and anonymizing, and handoff
scenes.narration: Case closed! Read the CSV, clean it, count with a dictionary, take a fair-share average that skips blanks, and label every bar. Now the most important part. Nova's survey asked first, let people pass, and had no names. That's consent and anonymity. Even without names, some answers together can point to one person, like the only thirteen-year-old in the chess club. Before sharing data, keep only the columns you need, replace names with IDs like R1 and R2, and never collect addresses, schools, birthdays or photos. Now open Exercise 8.1, the Survey cleaner, and type along with your teacher. Spot the mess in favorite_games.csv, then clean it until the Shell says Clean answers: seventeen. Happy detecting!

End card points to the Exercise 8.1 folder.
