videos.title: How Do Machines Learn?
videos.lesson_question: How can a program learn from labeled examples, and why does it copy their mistakes?
objectives: Explain the difference between a program with hand-written rules and one that learns from labeled examples.
Use the steps distance (gap plus gap) to find a mystery example's nearest neighbor.
Show how unbalanced training data leads to bad, unfair predictions.
Explain how a Markov text generator picks the next word, and why chatbots can sound sure and still be wrong.
videos.misconception: An AI understands what it says and is always fair, so when its guesses are wrong the bug must be in the code.
videos.safety_and_citizenship: AI ethics: AI can be wrong, even when it sounds sure, so check important facts with a trusted source or adult. Never type your real name, address, school, passwords, photos or secrets into a chatbot; what you type may be stored. Deepfakes are fake pictures, voices or videos made by AI: ask ‘Who made this, and why?’ before you believe or share, and never make fakes of real people. Bias: AI is only as fair as its examples. Final project kickoff: Build Something Big starts with your pitch (M1).
videos.lesson_handoff: Type along with your teacher in Exercise 9.1 Monster sorter: finish distance(a, b) with the steps distance (the gap in fluff plus the gap in teeth) and nearest(training, mystery), then run it to see each mystery ? joined to its nearest card. Then, in pairs, test fair and biased training in 9.2, build the Markov story machine in 9.3, and start your Build Something Big pitch card (workbook Exercise 9.4, Milestone 1).

scenes.purpose: Mission hook
scenes.narration: Pixel has a new job: sorting dragon eggs into fire eggs and ice eggs. But nobody wrote any rules! ‘Just learn from these examples,’ says Nova, and sets down a basket of labeled eggs. ‘Learn?’ beeps Pixel. ‘I only follow instructions!’ Can a program really learn from examples? And what if the examples are wrong?
scenes.visual: A basket of speckled eggs, each with a tag reading FIRE or ICE (a flame or snowflake symbol plus the word). Pixel searches an empty rulebook, then stares at the basket. Freeze on a question mark above Pixel.
scenes.production_notes: Every egg label uses a word and a symbol, never color alone.

scenes.purpose: Explain rules versus learning, features, labels and testing
scenes.narration: So far, your programs follow rules you typed: if teeth is more than five, say grumpy. A learning program is different. It gets examples with the right answers, called labels, and finds the pattern itself. The things it measures are called features. Our dragon eggs have two features: spots and size, each from zero to ten. Put every example on a chart. To guess a mystery egg, find the closest example and copy its label. That's a nearest-neighbor classifier. To check it, we hide some examples in a test pile, train on the rest, and count the right guesses: its accuracy. Testing on examples it learned from would be like seeing the exam answers first!
scenes.visual: Split screen: a 'Rules' card with an if-line versus a 'Learning' card with a stack of labeled examples. Eggs fly onto a feature chart (spots across, size up, 0 to 10), fire eggs as circles marked F, ice eggs as squares marked I. A deck splits into a big Training pile and a small face-down Test pile.
on_screen_text: Nearest neighbor: copy the closest label
Train on one pile, test on another
scenes.production_notes: Match the lesson's words: rules, examples, labels, features, training, test, accuracy.

scenes.purpose: Worked example: steps distance and a tiny Markov chain
scenes.narration: Here's a mystery egg: seven spots, size three. Which example is closest? Pretend each egg is a game piece on the grid from week seven. It can only step across or up and down, never on a slant. So the steps distance is the gap in spots plus the gap in size. A gap is the bigger number minus the smaller one. To the fire egg at eight, two, the gaps are one and one: two steps. To the ice egg at three, seven, the gaps are four and four: eight steps. The fire egg is closer, so the guess is fire! Machines can learn words, too. A Markov chain learns one thing: after each word, which words came next? From ‘my dog ran, my dog hid,’ it learns that after dog came ran or hid. Then it writes by picking a random next word, again and again. It sounds right, but understands nothing.
scenes.visual: Feature chart with four example eggs: fire at (8, 2) and (9, 4), ice at (2, 8) and (3, 7). A white ? egg sits at (7, 3). A dashed grid path walks 1 across and 1 down to (8, 2) with a '2 steps' label; another path walks 4 across and 4 up to (3, 7) with '8 steps'. The nearest egg gets a circle and the guess 'fire'. Then the training text 'my dog ran my dog hid' (shown without commas) becomes a word-chain: 'my' → 'dog'; 'dog' → 'ran' and 'hid'; 'ran' → 'my'. A spinner picks the next word and a silly sentence builds itself.
scenes.production_notes: Use the dragon-egg cards and the dog sentence only: never the monster cards, the (3, 6) or (5, 5) workbook questions, the exercise's story text, or the distance, nearest or build_chain code.

scenes.purpose: Friendly bug hunt: bad training data, bad predictions
scenes.narration: Bug hunt! Someone collected new training eggs but met only one fire egg, a very unusual one at ten spots, size zero, plus lots of ice eggs. Pixel tests it on four eggs it has never seen, and every fire egg gets labeled ice! Is the bug in the code, or in the data? Let's use our steps. Read: there's no red error at all. Predict. ‘The code runs fine. I think the examples are the problem,’ says Nova. Watch one guess on the chart. A real fire egg is six steps from that lonely fire example, but only four steps from an ice egg, so it copies ice. That's bias: unbalanced examples make unfair guesses. When a learning program is wrong, check the examples before the code. Fix one thing: add more fire examples. Check: test again, and the fire eggs are labeled fire.
scenes.visual: Training chart: one fire circle far away at (10, 0) and six ice squares at (2, 8), (3, 7), (2, 9), (4, 6), (3, 9) and (5, 5). Four test eggs appear: fire at (7, 3) and (6, 2), ice at (2, 7) and (3, 8). Both fire eggs get an 'ice' guess with a red X, while the ice eggs get green checks. For the fire egg at (7, 3), steps paths compare 3 + 3 = 6 steps (to the lonely fire egg) with 2 + 2 = 4 steps (to the ice egg at (5, 5)). A scale tips heavily toward ice. Three more fire examples join at (8, 2), (9, 4) and (7, 1), and both fire test eggs flip to fire with green checks.
on_screen_text: Is the bug in the code or the data?
Check the examples before the code
scenes.production_notes: Four-second prediction pause before Nova's line. Do not say any accuracy percentages from Exercise 9.2 or the exit ticket's 9-out-of-10 answer; do not reuse the lesson's (7, 3, "friendly") label swap.

scenes.purpose: Recap, AI ethics, project kickoff and handoff
scenes.narration: Door nine unlocked! A learning program finds patterns in labeled examples. Features are what it measures, the steps distance finds the nearest example, and a test pile checks its accuracy. But AI copies the mistakes in its examples. AI can be wrong, even when it sounds sure: check important facts with a trusted source or adult. Never type your real name, address, school, passwords, photos or secrets into a chatbot; what you type may be stored. Deepfakes are fake pictures, voices or videos: ask, ‘Who made this, and why?’ and never make fakes of real people. AI is only as fair as its examples. Now open Exercise 9.1, the Monster sorter, and type along with your teacher. Then start your Build Something Big pitch card!
scenes.visual: Mission map: door 9 opens. Four ethics cards flip over: Can be wrong, Keep it private, Spot deepfakes, Check for bias. A project road map appears with M1 Pitch glowing as the first stop, then M2 to M4 and the Showcase. End card points to the Exercise 9.1 folder.
on_screen_text: Wrong • Private • Fake • Unfair: be AI-wise
NEXT: 9.1 Monster sorter, then M1 Pitch
scenes.production_notes: No real chatbot logos or online services. End card includes ‘Narration uses an AI-generated voice’ and a five-second hold.

videos.title: Project Studio 1: Design First
videos.lesson_question: How do we plan a big project with classes, milestones and save points before we build it?
objectives: Design a project with CRC cards and a class diagram that shows ‘is a’ and ‘has a’ links.
Name the project's must-haves, its milestones and the Core or Full path.
Start a git repository for the project and make small commits with verb-first messages.
Check whether a picture, sound or library may be used, and give credit for it.
videos.misconception: Real programmers start typing right away and save everything in one big commit at the end, or inheritance fits every link between two classes.
videos.safety_and_citizenship: Licenses: may I use this? Everything in your project must be yours or allowed. The Python standard library is free to use, and your own drawings and sounds are yours. For someone else's picture or sound, look for its license: CC0 means free for anyone; CC BY means free if you give credit; ‘All rights reserved’ or no license means no. Never download anything without your parent, and write every borrowed thing in the Credits section of your README. Easiest choice: draw everything with turtle.
videos.lesson_handoff: Computers closed: write one CRC card per class for your own project (at least two classes; one uses inheritance or composition), play one turn by holding up each card as it does its job, and copy them into workbook Exercise 10.1. Then draw your class diagram (10.2), copy the starter folder into Documents/coding-projects and rename it, check the folder with pwd, run git init, write class skeletons and commit after each class (Milestone 2).

scenes.purpose: Studio hook
scenes.narration: Nova's pitch card says: Bee Garden, a grid game where a bee collects pollen and dodges wasps. Nova opens Thonny and starts typing as fast as possible. ‘Wait!’ beeps Pixel. ‘Which parts are there? Who does what?’ Builders draw plans before they pour concrete. Today we design first. What's your plan?
scenes.visual: Nova's pitch card fills the screen, then Nova types furiously while code lines tangle into a knot. Pixel holds up a blank index card. A builder's blueprint unrolls behind them.
on_screen_text: Pause: What parts does your project need?
scenes.production_notes: Bee Garden is Nova's own example; it is not the reference project.

scenes.purpose: Explain the brief: must-haves, paths and milestones
scenes.narration: Your final project, Build Something Big, can be a grid game, a generative art app, or a data or AI app. It needs two or more classes, one using inheritance or composition. It needs a data structure beyond a flat list, like a dictionary, a queue or a grid. Add one named algorithm, a saved file, five or more pytest tests, eight or more meaningful commits, and a README. It must be fair and safe, too. Most people take the Core path: start from a template, add one class of your own, reuse an algorithm from class, and save one file. The template's tests count toward your five. The Full path is extra challenge: your own design. The milestones are Pitch, Design and core classes, Features with five tests and a playtest, README and polish, and the Showcase.
scenes.visual: Three option doors: Grid game, Generative art app, Data/AI app. A must-have checklist ticks in one line at a time, ending with 'README' and 'Fair and safe'. A fork in the road labeled Core path (recommended) and Full path (extra challenge). A project road map lights up five stops: M1 Pitch ✓, M2 Design + core classes, M3 Features + 5 tests + playtest, M4 README + polish, Showcase.
scenes.production_notes: Milestone names and must-haves exactly as in the project brief. Do not show the Core path classes (Game, Tree, Guesser) as code.

scenes.purpose: Worked example: CRC cards, class diagram and first commit
scenes.narration: Let's design Bee Garden. A CRC card is an index card for one class: the Class name on top, its Responsibilities on the left, what it knows and does, and its Collaborators on the right, the classes it works with. Bee: knows its row and column, moves unless a wall is in the way, collects pollen. It works with Garden. Garden: holds the grid and says if a square is a wall. Now the class diagram. A hollow arrow means ‘is a’: a Bee is a Critter, and so is a Wasp. A diamond line means ‘has a’: the Game has a Garden and a Bee. Then, in Terminal, inside the project folder: git init, git add, and git commit with a message that starts with a verb, like ‘Add empty Garden and Bee classes.’ Git writes your name into every save point, so use your nickname, never your real name.
scenes.visual: Index cards fill in by hand: 'Class: Bee' with responsibilities on the left and 'Garden' as collaborator on the right; then 'Class: Garden'. The cards slide into a class diagram: Bee and Wasp each point to Critter with a hollow-triangle arrow labeled 'is a'; Game connects to Garden and Bee with diamond lines labeled 'has a'. A Terminal panel types: git init, git add bee_garden.py, git commit -m "Add empty Garden and Bee classes", git log --oneline. The commit's author reads a nickname with a placeholder example.com email.
on_screen_text: Hollow arrow = is a • Diamond = has a
scenes.production_notes: Never show Maze Muncher's CRC cards, class diagram, code or git log; use the Bee Garden example only. Show the author line as a nickname, never a real name.

scenes.purpose: Friendly bug hunt: partner code review
scenes.narration: Time for a partner code review! Partners swap seats and read each other's code using three questions. One: does every class match a CRC card? Two: is there a method that does two jobs? Three: is there a name I don't understand? Pixel reviews Nova's code. A Wasp is a Critter, but its init only sets speed. Pixel runs it. Read the last line of the error: AttributeError, Wasp object has no attribute row. Predict. ‘I think Wasp never ran Critter's init,’ says Nova. Fix one thing: add super, dot, init, with row and col, as the first line. Check: run it again. Now the wasp knows where it is! Pixel writes one star, ‘Clear class names,’ and one wish: ‘Add a test for Wasp.’
scenes.visual: Two seats swap. A review card shows the three questions. Code panel: class Critter with __init__(self, row, col) setting self.row and self.col; class Wasp(Critter) whose __init__ only sets self.speed = 1. The Shell shows the red AttributeError. The step cards light up: Read, Predict, Watch, Fix ONE thing, Check. The line super().__init__(row, col) slides in at the top of Wasp's __init__; the rerun prints the row. A star sticky note and a wish sticky note appear.
on_screen_text: 3 review questions: card? two jobs? name?
scenes.production_notes: Model kind, specific feedback about the code, never the person. Four-second pause before the fix.

scenes.purpose: Recap, licenses and handoff
scenes.narration: Design done! CRC cards say what each class knows and does. The class diagram shows ‘is a’ and ‘has a.’ Milestones are like LEGO bags, and each commit is a photo after a bag. Now, may you use that picture or sound? Everything in your project must be yours or allowed. Python's standard library is free, and your own drawings are yours. CC0 means free for anyone. CC BY means free if you give credit. All rights reserved, or no license, means no. Never download without a parent, and list borrowed things in your README's Credits. Easiest choice: draw it with turtle! Now grab index cards: one CRC card per class. Play one turn, draw your diagram, then git init and commit your class skeletons.
scenes.visual: LEGO bags numbered 1 to 4, each followed by a camera flash labeled 'commit'. Three license badges: CC0 (green check), CC BY (check plus 'give credit'), All rights reserved (stop sign). A README 'Credits' section fills in. End card: index cards, a class diagram and a Terminal with git init.
on_screen_text: CC0 = free • CC BY = free + credit
NEXT: CRC cards → diagram → git init
scenes.production_notes: No real logos or brands. End card includes ‘Narration uses an AI-generated voice’ and a five-second hold.

videos.title: Project Studio 2: Test and Polish
videos.lesson_question: How do we prove our project works, learn from playtesters, and explain it to a stranger?
objectives: Write pytest tests for your own classes, including an edge case, and check that a test can fail.
Run a playtest and sort the problems into Must fix, Should fix and Nice to have.
List what a README needs: what it is, how to run it, how it works, tests and credits.
Check a project for accessibility and usability and fix at least one problem.
videos.misconception: If the program works when I play it, it has no bugs, or a test that passes must be checking something.
videos.safety_and_citizenship: Accessibility and usability review: colors from the Okabe–Ito palette and never color alone (add shapes, letters or text); text large enough to read from a chair; controls written on screen; no fast flashing; usability: a new player knows what to do within 10 seconds. Credits: every borrowed image or sound is listed with its license (or there are none).
videos.lesson_handoff: Milestone 3: plan and write at least five tests in test_<your project>.py (at least one edge case; on the Core path the template's passing tests count), run python -m pytest -q in Thonny's system shell and commit when green. Then do the playtest swap with feedback cards and sort them into Must fix, Should fix and Nice to have, and fix one must-fix with a test first. Then Milestone 4: README.md, the accessibility check and one fix.

scenes.purpose: Studio hook
scenes.narration: Bee Garden runs! Nova is ready to show everyone. Then Pixel walks the bee into the corner of the garden… and the whole game crashes. ‘But it worked when I played it!’ says Nova. Other people press keys you'd never think of. How can we catch bugs like this before the showcase?
scenes.visual: Bee Garden on a grid: Pixel steers the bee into the bottom-right corner, the window freezes and a red error pops up. Nova's jaw drops. A calendar shows 'Showcase' circled.
on_screen_text: Pause: How can we find them first?
scenes.production_notes: Comic, not scary: a soft bonk, not a crash siren.

scenes.purpose: Explain tests, edge cases, playtests and READMEs
scenes.narration: Today has three jobs. First, tests: tiny programs that check your program. They're like crash-test dummies for cars. You can break things on purpose, safely, as often as you like. Test the logic, like moving and scoring, not the drawing. And test normal cases and edge cases: the corner, the wall, the empty list, the last life. Second, a playtest: someone else uses your project while you watch silently and take notes. Every time they get stuck, you learn something. Third, a README: it tells a stranger what your project is, how to run it, how it works, and who you thank. Future-you is a stranger too!
scenes.visual: A crash-test dummy rides a tiny car into a wall and pops back up smiling. Edge cases glow on a grid: a corner square, a wall, an empty list [ ], a single heart. A playtester plays while the owner zips their lips and writes notes. A README page fills in section headings.
on_screen_text: Edge cases: corner, wall, empty, last life
scenes.production_notes: Keep the words test, edge case, playtest and README as in the lesson.

scenes.purpose: Worked example: two tests for a tiny Bee class
scenes.narration: Let's test a tiny Bee class. A new bee has three lives. lose_life takes one away, and if lives drop below zero, it sets them back to zero. Nova writes two tests, and each name says what it checks. Test one: a new bee starts with three lives. Test two is an edge case: lose five lives in a row, and lives should stop at zero. In Thonny's system shell, type python, dash m, pytest, dash q. Two dots: two passing tests! But is test two any good? Break the code on purpose. Nova deletes the two lines that stop at zero, and runs again. An F appears, with the name: lives never go below zero. The test caught it! Put the lines back, green again, and commit: ‘Add tests for Bee lives.’
scenes.visual: Code panel bee_garden.py: class Bee with __init__ setting self.lives = 3, and lose_life doing self.lives -= 1, then if self.lives < 0: self.lives = 0. Second panel test_bee_garden.py: from bee_garden import Bee; def test_bee_starts_with_3_lives(): assert Bee().lives == 3; def test_lives_never_go_below_zero(): bee = Bee(), a for-loop calling bee.lose_life() five times, assert bee.lives == 0. Shell: python -m pytest -q prints '..' and '2 passed'. The two guard lines get deleted; rerun shows '.F' and the failing test name in red. Lines restored; '2 passed' again; git commit -m "Add tests for Bee lives".
on_screen_text: Break it on purpose: does it go red?
Test names say what they check
scenes.production_notes: Use this Bee example, not the workbook's tiny Player tests or the template's tests. All code must stay exactly valid as written in the visual.

scenes.purpose: Friendly bug hunt: playtest bug triage
scenes.narration: Playtest time! Pixel plays Bee Garden for three minutes, thinking out loud, while Nova stays silent and writes one feedback card per thing: what happened, and what did the player expect? The cards say: the game crashes in the corner. Pollen and wasps look the same. And, ‘I wish there were sound effects.’ Now triage: sort the cards into three piles. Must fix: crashes, can't start, can't win. Should fix: confusing, unfair, hard to read. Nice to have: new ideas for version two. Which pile does the crash go in? Pause and decide. Yes, must fix! For a crash, first write a test that shows the bug, then fix it, so it never comes back. Commit: ‘Fix crash when the bee walks into the corner.’
scenes.visual: Pixel plays with a speech bubble of thoughts; Nova's lips are zipped while three feedback cards fill in under the headings 'What happened?' and 'What did the player expect?'. Three labeled piles appear: 1 Must fix, 2 Should fix, 3 Nice to have. The cards fly to their piles: crash → Must fix, look-alike pollen and wasps → Should fix, sound effects → Nice to have. A new red test appears, then turns green after the fix, then a commit line.
on_screen_text: Must fix • Should fix • Nice to have
Crash? Write a test first, then fix
scenes.production_notes: Four-second pause before revealing the crash's pile. The owner stays silent during the playtest.

scenes.purpose: Recap, accessibility and usability review, and handoff
scenes.narration: Project leveled up! Tests are crash-test dummies, edge cases hide in corners, and triage means fixing the most important thing first. Now the accessibility and usability check. Use colors from the Okabe-Ito palette, and never color alone: add shapes, letters or text. Make text big enough to read from a chair. Write the controls on screen. Nothing flashes fast. A new player should know what to do within ten seconds. And list every borrowed image or sound with its license. Now Milestone 3: write five tests, including an edge case, and commit when they pass. Then the playtest swap and triage. Then Milestone 4: your README and one accessibility fix.
scenes.visual: A checklist ticks: Okabe–Ito colors plus shapes and letters (pollen becomes a yellow circle with P, wasps a blue triangle with W), big text, controls on screen, no flashing, a 10-second timer. The road map highlights M3 and M4. End card: a test file, feedback cards and a README.
on_screen_text: Never color alone: add shapes or letters
Big text • Controls on screen • No flashing
NEXT: M3 tests → playtest → M4 README
scenes.production_notes: Do not show fast flashing even as a bad example. End card includes ‘Narration uses an AI-generated voice’ and a five-second hold.

videos.title: Showcase and Graduation
videos.lesson_question: How do we share what we built, explain why we built it that way, and keep coding safely?
objectives: Plan a two-minute talk that explains one design decision with Problem, Choice, Why and Next time.
Give kind, specific and useful feedback with one star and one wish.
Describe how the gallery walk, the talks and the exit assessment work.
Name safe ways to keep learning and to join coding communities together with a parent.
videos.misconception: A showcase talk should list every feature, and a crash during the demo ruins it.
videos.safety_and_citizenship: Showcase safety and next steps online: show your nickname, never your real name, on screen; projects stay on our computers and are not uploaded; photos or videos only if everyone agrees. If you share your work later: share with family, or post only with a parent, never with your real name, school, face or location. Choose any coding community together with a parent: look for clear rules, moderators and a code of conduct, and use a nickname. Never move to private chats with strangers, never send photos, and tell an adult if anything feels wrong.
videos.lesson_handoff: Set up your showcase station: your project and a Terminal showing git log --oneline side by side, with the talk card you filled in for homework 11 (workbook Exercise 12.1: Problem, Choice, Why, Next time) ready. Then join the gallery walk: try every project and leave a feedback card with one star and one wish, face down. Then give your 2-minute talk with a timekeeper and a questioner, and take the exit assessment.

scenes.purpose: Showcase hook
scenes.narration: The whole Kids Coding workshop has turned into a gallery, and every station runs a project someone built. Nova has two minutes to present Bee Garden. ‘I'll show all forty features!’ says Nova. Pixel's timer beeps. Hmm. In two minutes, what's the most interesting thing you could tell people about your project?
scenes.visual: Workshop doors fold back into a gallery of glowing project stations, each with a nickname card. Nova unrolls a very long feature list; Pixel holds up a 2:00 timer. Freeze on a thinking bubble.
scenes.production_notes: Keep the timer calm and noncompetitive. Only nicknames on station cards.

scenes.purpose: Explain a design-decision talk
scenes.narration: Anyone can say what their program does. A real developer can explain why they built it that way. That's a design decision: a choice about how to build something, with a reason. A museum guide doesn't read every label. They stop at one painting and tell you why the artist painted it that way. So pick one decision and walk through four steps. Problem: what was hard or not working? Choice: what did you decide to do? Why: why that way, and not another? Next time: what would you change? Great decisions to talk about: inheritance or composition, a dictionary or a grid, which algorithm, or what a test caught.
scenes.visual: A museum guide stops at one painting while others blur. Four story cards slide in left to right: 1 Problem, 2 Choice, 3 Why, 4 Next time, joined by arrows. Small idea chips float below: is a / has a, dict or grid, algorithm, a test that caught a bug.
on_screen_text: Design decision = a choice + a reason
scenes.production_notes: Use the four-step wording from the workbook.

scenes.purpose: Demo and explain: Nova's model talk
scenes.narration: Let's hear Nova's talk. ‘This is Bee Garden. You collect all the pollen without bumping into a wasp.’ Nova plays for twenty seconds. ‘Problem: my bee and my wasps needed the same position and moving code, and I was copying it twice. Choice: I made a Critter class, and Bee and Wasp are each a Critter. Why: inheritance keeps the shared code in one place, so a fix happens once. Another way was copy and paste, but then every bug needs fixing twice. A test caught a real bug, too: lives dropping below zero. Next time, I'd add a second level loaded from a file.’ Then Nova shows git log, and the save points tell the story, step by step. ‘Any questions?’
scenes.visual: Nova stands beside a running Bee Garden window (bee B, pollen P, wasps W). The four story cards light up one at a time as Nova speaks. A small class diagram shows Bee and Wasp pointing to Critter with 'is a' arrows; a copy-paste icon gets crossed out. A green test row flashes. A Terminal shows git log --oneline with short verb-first messages scrolling up.
on_screen_text: Choice: Bee and Wasp are Critters
Why: shared code in one place
Show git log: the story of your project
scenes.production_notes: Use Nova's Bee Garden talk, never the Maze Muncher model talk or its git log. Commit messages shown are generic Bee Garden steps that start with a verb.

scenes.purpose: Demo and explain: gallery walk, talks and exit assessment
scenes.narration: Now the gallery walk. Visit every station and try each project. On a feedback card, write one star, something specific you liked, and one wish, a specific idea. Good feedback is kind, specific and useful. ‘Cool!’ is kind, but not useful. ‘The score text was big and easy to read’ is all three. Then the talks. One listener is the timekeeper, and another asks one question that starts with ‘Why did you…?’ What if your demo crashes? That's normal! Smile, say, ‘That's a bug for the next version,’ and show your code or your tests instead. Last comes the exit assessment. You work alone and quietly, and it shows what you've learned in Level 3.
scenes.visual: Learners walk between stations, leaving feedback cards face down: a star line and a wish line. A vague card 'Cool!' gets an upgrade to the specific sentence. A timekeeper raises a hand at 1:30; a questioner's speech bubble starts 'Why did you…?'. A demo window shows a friendly error and the presenter switches calmly to a test file. A quiet desk with a paper and pencil closes the scene.
on_screen_text: Demo crashed? Show the code or tests
scenes.production_notes: No phones or cameras pointed at screens. Do not show or describe any exit assessment questions.

scenes.purpose: Celebration, safe next steps online, and handoff
scenes.narration: Level 3 complete! You saved your work with git, built classes, searched and sorted, drew fractals, cleaned data, trained a tiny AI, and built something big. Want to keep coding? Your project is yours. If you share it, share with family, or post only with a parent, never with your real name, school, face or location. Choose any coding community with a parent: look for clear rules, moderators and a code of conduct, and use a nickname. Never move to private chats with strangers, never send photos, and tell an adult if anything feels wrong. Now set up your station with your talk card ready: Problem, Choice, Why, Next time. Then join the gallery walk with a star and a wish for every project. Happy coding, graduate!
scenes.visual: A Level 3 timeline lights up stop by stop: git save points, classes, search and sort, recursion and grids, data and AI, my big project. A safety shield checks: nickname, parent, rules and moderators, no private chats. A graduation cap lands on Pixel. End card shows a talk card (Problem, Choice, Why, Next time) beside a star-and-wish feedback card.
on_screen_text: No private chats • No photos to strangers
scenes.production_notes: Warm celebration music with room for applause. The talk card was homework 11; this end card points to the gallery walk. End card includes ‘Narration uses an AI-generated voice’ and a five-second hold.
